approachQuestion.prompt: An editor must keep exactly k entries from an integer sequence, preserving their original order. Return the lexicographically smallest possible kept sequence: at the first differing position, the smaller integer wins. Equal entries are allowed; 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Example: values [4, 2, 3, 1, 5] with k=3 returns [2, 1, 5]. With [2, 2, 1] and k=2, return [2, 1]. Choose the best approach.
constraints: The input is immutable; n is between 1 and 200,000. All integers, indices, counts, and arithmetic results fit in signed 64-bit machine words; comparisons and arithmetic have unit cost.
Input and returned output are excluded from auxiliary space. Working stacks, arrays, and copies count. No hashing is used.

options.text: Scan positions i from left to right with a stack capped at k entries. While its top exceeds values[i] and (stack size - 1) + (n - i) is at least k, pop. Then push values[i] only if the stack has fewer than k entries.
options.feedback: Replacing a larger trailing value improves the earliest changed position. The remaining-count test includes the current entry and ensures that each removal still permits a length-k answer. Keeping an equal earlier value preserves at least as many future choices.

options.text: Always pop larger trailing entries before adding the current value, ignoring how many entries remain; trim the final stack to k.
options.feedback: The answer may become too short. For [3, 2, 1] and k=2, this leaves only [1]. Trimming cannot restore discarded entries.

options.text: Sort a copy of all values and return its k smallest entries.
options.feedback: Sorting violates the required order. For [2, 1] and k=2, the only legal result is [2, 1], not [1, 2].

options.text: For each output position, scan the remaining feasible index range to select its smallest value, taking the earliest minimum, and continue after it.
options.feedback: This is correct, but repeatedly scans overlapping candidate ranges; with equal values and k near n/2, it performs quadratic work. The stack avoids those repeated searches.

feedback.reason: Discard a dominated suffix only when enough unprocessed entries remain to complete the required length.
details: Keep at most k tentative entries. Before accepting the current entry, remove larger trailing entries only while the stack size after removal plus the number of entries from the current index through the end can still reach k. Append if there is room. Copy the final k entries into the returned array once.

Remove a larger tentative tail only when remaining entries can still fill k slots. Lexicographic improvement does not justify producing too short a result. Equal values need not replace earlier equal choices.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For feasible-suffix-replacement, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the input length and k the required output length. Keep a separate growable working stack capped at k entries, then copy its k entries once into the returned array; count that copy in time but exclude the returned array from space.
constraints: Stack push, pop, and top take amortized constant time using a growable array; each entry uses a constant number of words. Count the working stack, but exclude input and final output. No recursive call stack or hash table is used.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(k) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each tentative entry is pushed/popped at most once in a size-k working stack.
details: Every input entry is inspected once and pushed at most once; each pushed entry is popped at most once. Copying the final k entries costs O(k), which is within O(n). The separate working stack holds at most k entries and reaches k, so its tight auxiliary bound is O(k).
